entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Enough for a particular purpose or need; as much as is required, but not necessarily more.
entries.usage: More formal than *enough*; common in official letters, legal language, reports and instructions: *sufficient evidence*, *sufficient funds*, *sufficient time*. Typical patterns are *sufficient for* + noun and *sufficient to* + verb. In casual speech *enough* sounds more natural, and *insufficient* is the opposite (*insufficient funds* on a bank notice).
entries.pattern: sufficient evidence / funds / time; sufficient for + noun; sufficient to + verb
examples: The judge ruled that there wasn't **sufficient** evidence to go to trial.
Please make sure there are **sufficient** funds in your account before the payment date.
Two hours should be **sufficient** for most visitors to see the whole museum.

drill.sentence: One letter from her doctor was {{sufficient}} to get her out of jury duty this year.
drill.hint: formal adjective: as much as was needed (not *enough* or *adequate*)

entries.related: *enough* — the everyday word; *adequate* — enough, or just good enough; *ample* — more than enough; *insufficient* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Seeming to be true or real, although it may not be (*her apparent calm*); or clearly visible and obvious (*for no apparent reason*).
entries.usage: Before a noun it usually means *seeming*, and news reports use it when facts are not yet confirmed: *an apparent accident*, *his apparent lack of interest*. After *be* or *become* it usually means *obvious*: *It soon became apparent that …*. The fixed phrase *for no apparent reason* is very common in speech.
entries.pattern: it becomes / is apparent that …; for no apparent reason; an apparent + noun (= seeming)
examples: Halfway through the trip, it became **apparent** that we'd packed way too much.
The dog started barking for no **apparent** reason in the middle of the night.
Fire officials say the blaze was started by an **apparent** electrical problem in the kitchen.

drill.sentence: Her {{apparent}} lack of interest in the job offer turned out to be a negotiating tactic.
drill.hint: how it looked from the outside (not *seeming*, *obvious*, *supposed* or *feigned*)

entries.related: *apparently* — the adverb, often means *I've heard that*; *obvious* — clearly true, no doubt; *evident* — clear from the evidence, more formal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Continuing at the present time and not finished yet; still in progress.
entries.usage: Very common in news, work and official language: *an ongoing investigation*, *ongoing talks*, *ongoing problems*, *an ongoing process*. It works before a noun and after *be*; *The investigation is ongoing* is the standard phrase of police and press officers. It is written as one word, without a hyphen.
entries.pattern: an ongoing investigation / problem / process / project; be ongoing
examples: Police wouldn't say much about the case because the investigation is **ongoing**.
My knee has been an **ongoing** problem since I hurt it playing soccer in college.
Learning a language is an **ongoing** process; you never really finish.

drill.sentence: The city says the {{ongoing}} construction on Main Street will last until at least next spring.
drill.hint: still in progress now (one word; not *continuing* or *current*)

entries.related: *continuing* — similar, a bit more formal; *in progress* — after the noun (*work in progress*); *current* — happening now, not necessarily for long.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make it possible for someone or something to do something, by giving them the means, the ability or the opportunity.
entries.usage: Common in business, tech and formal writing; in conversation *let* is more usual. Use *enable* + object + *to* + verb (*enables you to pay*) or *enable* + noun (*enables faster checkout*); the object cannot be dropped. In software, *enable a setting* means turn it on, and in everyday talk *enabling* someone means supporting their bad habits.
entries.pattern: enable someone / something to + verb; enable + noun
examples: A small scholarship **enabled** her to spend a semester in Spain.
Remote work has **enabled** many families to move out of expensive cities.
Contactless payment **enables** faster checkout, which is why stores love it.

drill.sentence: Hearing aids have {{enabled}} my grandfather to enjoy family dinners again.
drill.hint: made it possible for (not *allowed* or *helped*)

mistake.wrong: This app enables to track your spending.
mistake.right: This app enables you to track your spending.
mistake.why: *Enable* needs an object before *to*: *enable someone to do something*.

entries.related: *allow* — permit, or make possible; *let* — casual, with no *to* (*lets you pay*); *empower* — give power or confidence; *prevent* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A list of topics to discuss at a meeting; also the set of goals a person or group is trying to achieve, sometimes secretly.
entries.usage: In offices: *on the agenda*, *the first item on the agenda*, *set the agenda*, *send out the agenda*. *A hidden agenda* or *have an agenda* suggests a secret, selfish purpose, so saying someone *has an agenda* is an accusation. *What's on the agenda?* is also a casual way to ask about plans for the day or weekend.
entries.pattern: on the agenda; set / send out the agenda; a hidden agenda; have an agenda
examples: The budget is the first item on the **agenda** for Monday's meeting.
I don't trust his sudden interest in helping; I think he has an **agenda**.
So, what's on the **agenda** for this weekend? Anything fun?

drill.sentence: She offered to help with the school fundraiser, but some parents suspected a hidden {{agenda}}.
drill.hint: a secret purpose she wasn't sharing (not *motive*)

entries.related: *schedule* — the times of events; *program* — the order of events at a show; *ulterior motive* — a hidden reason, close to *hidden agenda*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Able to be trusted to work well, behave as expected or give correct information, again and again.
entries.usage: Used for people, machines, sources and data: *a reliable car*, *reliable information*, *a reliable source*, *reliable public transit*. It stresses consistency over time, which makes it a strong compliment for an employee or a coworker. The noun is *reliability*; *dependable* is close and a little warmer.
entries.pattern: a reliable source / car / employee; reliable information / data
examples: My old Honda isn't pretty, but it's the most **reliable** car I've ever owned.
Is there a **reliable** way to get to the airport at 5 a.m. without a car?
I heard from a **reliable** source that the diner on Fifth Street is closing next month.

drill.sentence: We need a babysitter who's {{reliable}}; the last one canceled on us three times in a month.
drill.hint: who always shows up as promised (not *dependable*, *responsible* or *trustworthy*)

entries.related: *dependable* — very close, a bit warmer; *trustworthy* — honest, can be trusted with secrets or money; *unreliable* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Clearly different or separate from something else; also clearly noticeable (*a distinct smell*).
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *two distinct groups*, *distinct from*, *a distinct possibility*, *a distinct advantage*. Do not mix it up with *distinctive*, which means typical of one person or thing and easy to recognize (*a distinctive voice*). *As distinct from* is a formal way to say *as opposed to*.
entries.pattern: distinct from + noun; two / three distinct + plural noun; a distinct possibility / advantage
examples: The twins look alike, but they have very **distinct** personalities.
There's a **distinct** smell of smoke in the hallway, so I'm calling the building manager.
Pack a rain jacket; afternoon storms are a **distinct** possibility in the mountains.

drill.sentence: The Spanish spoken in Argentina is quite {{distinct}} from the Spanish of Mexico, especially in its rhythm.
drill.hint: clearly not the same as the other (not *different* or *separate*)

entries.related: *distinctive* — typical and easy to recognize; *separate* — not joined; *clear* — easy to notice; *indistinct* — the opposite, hard to see or hear.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A basic structure of ideas, rules or principles that you use to plan, judge or organize something.
entries.usage: Common in work, policy and academic language: *a framework for* + noun or *-ing*, *a legal framework*, *a theoretical framework*, *within the framework of*. In software, a *framework* is a ready-made structure of code that you build on. It sounds formal; in conversation people may say *structure* or *system*.
entries.pattern: a framework for + noun / -ing; a legal / theoretical framework; within the framework of
examples: The treaty gives countries a **framework** for sharing water from the river during droughts.
The school uses a simple **framework** for resolving conflicts between students.
Most of the city's websites are built on the same open-source **framework**.

drill.sentence: Lawmakers are still working on a legal {{framework}} for drones that deliver packages.
drill.hint: basic structure of rules (not *basis* or *system*)

entries.related: *structure* — more general; *system* — a working set of parts or methods; *guidelines* — advice that is less fixed; *model* — a simplified example to copy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely important, because the result or success of something depends on it.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *a crucial role*, *a crucial moment*, *crucial for*, *crucial to*, *it is crucial that* + clause. It is stronger than *important* and close to *vital*, and it often points to a moment that decides the result. Since it is already strong, *absolutely crucial* sounds more natural than *very crucial*.
entries.pattern: crucial to / for + noun; it is crucial (that … / to + verb); a crucial role / moment / step
examples: The first 48 hours are **crucial** in any missing-person case.
His late goal was **crucial**; without it, the team would have missed the playoffs.
The next two weeks are **crucial** for farmers; without rain, much of the corn could fail.

drill.sentence: It's absolutely {{crucial}} to keep the cut clean and dry for the first few days.
drill.hint: extremely important for the result (not *vital*, *essential*, *critical*, *key* or *necessary*)

entries.related: *vital* — necessary for life or success; *critical* — crucial, or criticizing; *key* — informal and very common before nouns (*a key moment*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To keep trying to achieve something over a long time, such as a goal, a career, a degree or an idea.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *pursue a career in*, *pursue a degree*, *pursue your dreams*, *pursue a goal*, *pursue legal action*. It sounds more serious and committed than *go after* or *try for*. It also means *chase* (*Police pursued the car*), and the noun is *pursuit* (*the pursuit of happiness*).
entries.pattern: pursue a career (in) / a degree / a goal / an idea / legal action
examples: After ten years in banking, she quit to **pursue** a career in nursing.
He's **pursuing** a master's degree at night while working full time.
The family decided not to **pursue** legal action against the hospital.

drill.sentence: My parents wanted me to be a lawyer, but I decided to {{pursue}} my dream of becoming a chef.
drill.hint: work toward it seriously (not *follow*, *chase* or *fulfill*)

entries.related: *go after* — informal; *strive for* — formal, stresses effort; *pursuit* — the noun; *abandon* or *give up* — the opposites.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To meet or experience something, often a problem or difficulty, especially without planning or expecting it.
entries.usage: Common in formal and written English: *encounter problems*, *encounter difficulties*, *encounter resistance*, *encounter an error*. In everyday talk, *run into* or *come across* sounds more natural. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition, unlike the noun (*an encounter with a bear*).
entries.pattern: encounter problems / difficulties / resistance / an error
examples: If you **encounter** an error while filling out the form, try a different browser.
Hikers sometimes **encounter** black bears on this trail, so carry bear spray.
The plan to close the library **encountered** strong resistance from parents.

drill.sentence: On their first trip abroad, they {{encountered}} more problems than they'd expected, starting with a lost passport.
drill.hint: unexpectedly met (formal verb; not *had*, *faced* or *ran into*)

mistake.wrong: We encountered with a lot of problems on the trip.
mistake.right: We encountered a lot of problems on the trip.
mistake.why: The verb takes a direct object; *with* belongs only after the noun (*an encounter with*).

entries.related: *run into* / *come across* — informal; *face* — have to deal with, often known in advance; *experience* — more neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Felt or done equally by each of two or more people toward the other; also shared by both (*a mutual friend*).
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *mutual respect*, *mutual trust*, *by mutual agreement*, *a mutual friend*. The reply *The feeling is mutual* is common and can be warm or sarcastic. *Mutual* stresses that something goes both ways; for something simply shared by a group, *common* is usual (*a common goal*).
entries.pattern: mutual respect / trust / friend / interest; by mutual agreement; the feeling is mutual
examples: We met through a **mutual** friend at a barbecue in Austin.
The coach and his players have a lot of **mutual** respect.
She told him she'd never liked him, and he said the feeling was **mutual**.

drill.sentence: After eight years together, the couple decided to separate by {{mutual}} agreement, with no hard feelings.
drill.hint: shared equally by both of them (not *joint* or *common*)

mistake.wrong: We met through a common friend.
mistake.right: We met through a mutual friend.
mistake.why: For a person both of you know, the normal phrase is *mutual friend*; *common friend* sounds like a translation of German *gemeinsamer Freund*.

entries.related: *shared* — had by both, neutral; *common* — shared by a group (*a common goal*); *reciprocal* — formal, given in return; *one-sided* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Action taken by someone, often an authority or a professional, to change a situation, improve it or stop a problem from getting worse.
entries.usage: Used in news, medicine, education and policy: *government intervention*, *military intervention*, *medical intervention*, *early intervention*. In American everyday speech, *an intervention* is also a planned meeting where family and friends confront someone about an addiction. The verb is *intervene* (*intervene in a dispute*).
entries.pattern: early / government / medical intervention; intervention in + situation; stage an intervention
examples: Thanks to early **intervention**, the speech problems she had as a toddler are completely gone.
Most small kidney stones pass on their own, without medical **intervention**.
His friends staged an **intervention** because his drinking was getting out of control.

drill.sentence: The neighbors' shouting match only ended after police {{intervention}} at two in the morning.
drill.hint: stepping in to stop it (not *action* or *involvement*)

entries.related: *interference* — unwanted involvement, negative; *involvement* — taking part; *intervene* — the verb; *mediation* — a neutral person helping two sides agree.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The range of things that a project, study, law, job or discussion covers and deals with.
entries.usage: Common at work and in academic writing: *the scope of the project*, *broaden* or *narrow the scope*, *beyond the scope of*, *outside the scope of*, *out of scope*. *Scope creep* is office jargon for a project that slowly grows beyond what was agreed. *Scope for* + noun (mainly British) means opportunity; Americans usually say *room for improvement*.
entries.pattern: the scope of + noun; broaden / narrow the scope; beyond / outside the scope of; out of scope
examples: Fixing the roof wasn't in the original contract, so it's outside the **scope** of the job.
The investigation is limited in **scope**; it only looks at last year's spending.
Let's narrow the **scope** to one city before we try to cover the whole state.

drill.sentence: Questions about the new parking garage are beyond the {{scope}} of tonight's meeting, which is only about the school budget.
drill.hint: range of topics it covers (not *remit* or *purpose*)

entries.related: *range* — the spread between limits; *extent* — how large or far something is; *remit* — mainly British, the official tasks of a person or group; *room for* — space or chance for something.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Almost completely; so nearly that the difference does not matter.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, especially with absolute words: *virtually impossible*, *virtually identical*, *virtually everyone*, *virtually nothing*, *virtually unknown*. It is slightly more formal than *almost* or *practically*. Its other meaning, *online or by computer* (*attend virtually*), has become common with remote work, so context decides.
entries.pattern: virtually impossible / identical / unknown; virtually all / every / no / nothing
examples: With all the construction downtown, finding parking on a Saturday is **virtually** impossible.
The two phones are **virtually** identical except for the camera.
Before her novel won the prize, she was **virtually** unknown outside her hometown.

drill.sentence: The town is so small that {{virtually}} everyone knows who's dating whom.
drill.hint: so close to all that it doesn't matter (not *almost*, *nearly*, *basically* or *practically*)

entries.related: *practically* — the same, more casual; *almost* / *nearly* — neutral; *effectively* — in practice, though not officially; *virtual* — online, or almost.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make something start suddenly, such as a reaction, an event, an alarm or a strong emotion.
entries.usage: Very common in news, health and everyday speech: *trigger an alarm*, *trigger a migraine*, *trigger a reaction*, *trigger a debate*, *be triggered by*. It usually suggests that a small cause starts a big or automatic effect. *Triggered* also describes a person upset by something that reminds them of a bad experience, and online it is often used mockingly.
entries.pattern: trigger an alarm / a reaction / a migraine / a debate; be triggered by + noun
examples: Burning toast **triggered** the smoke alarm, and everyone in the building had to go outside.
For me, strong perfume can **trigger** a migraine within minutes.
Rumors that the bank was in trouble **triggered** a rush of customers trying to withdraw their money.

drill.sentence: Even a small earthquake can {{trigger}} a landslide on these steep, wet hillsides.
drill.hint: make happen all at once (not *cause*, *start* or *set off*)

entries.related: *set off* — phrasal verb, same meaning; *spark* — mostly for debates, protests and fires; *cause* — more general; *prompt* — lead someone to act.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Following the usual, traditional way of doing things rather than a new or unusual one; sometimes also too ordinary and not original.
entries.usage: Common in many fields: *conventional wisdom* (what most people believe), *conventional medicine*, *a conventional oven*, *conventional weapons*. About people and taste it can be mildly critical (*a very conventional choice*), suggesting a lack of imagination. The opposite, *unconventional*, often sounds like praise.
entries.pattern: conventional wisdom / methods / medicine / oven; by conventional standards
examples: Instead of a **conventional** wedding in a hotel ballroom, they got married on a hiking trail with six friends.
Bake the cookies for twelve minutes in a **conventional** oven, or ten in a convection oven.
Her parents wanted her to choose a more **conventional** career, like law or accounting.

drill.sentence: The {{conventional}} wisdom was that nobody would ever pay for bottled water, and look how that turned out.
drill.hint: adjective: what most people take for granted (not *common*, *popular*, *accepted* or *received*)

entries.related: *traditional* — based on long custom, often positive; *orthodox* — accepted, formal; *mainstream* — what most people do; *unconventional* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Large in size, amount, degree or importance; big enough to notice or to matter.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and formal speech: *considerable time*, *considerable effort*, *a considerable amount of*, *at considerable cost*, *considerable damage*. It is more formal than *a lot of* and sounds measured, not emotional. The adverb *considerably* is very common with comparatives: *considerably cheaper*, *considerably more*.
entries.pattern: considerable time / effort / damage; a considerable amount of; at considerable cost; considerably + comparative
examples: It took **considerable** effort to get the piano up three flights of stairs.
Learning to play the cello as an adult takes **considerable** patience.
They renovated the old farmhouse at **considerable** cost, then sold it a year later.

drill.sentence: The new stadium will bring a {{considerable}} amount of traffic to this quiet neighborhood on game days.
drill.hint: big enough to matter; formal (not *large*, *great*, *significant* or *substantial*)

mistake.wrong: It was very considerable of you to bring us dinner.
mistake.right: It was very considerate of you to bring us dinner.
mistake.why: *Considerate* means kind and thoughtful toward others; *considerable* means large.

entries.related: *substantial* — large and solid, very close; *significant* — large enough to matter, or important; *considerate* — kind, a different word; *negligible* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very varied; including many different types of people or things.
entries.usage: Common in news, schools, companies and travel writing: *a diverse group*, *a diverse city*, *diverse backgrounds*, *a diverse range of*. About people, in American usage it often refers to ethnic, racial or cultural variety. It stresses variety and difference, so it does not simply mean *several* or *various*, as German *diverse* does (*diverse Gründe* = *various reasons*).
entries.pattern: a diverse group / range / city; diverse backgrounds / interests
examples: Coral reefs are among the most **diverse** ecosystems on the planet.
Our book club is pretty **diverse**: a nurse, two retired teachers, a pilot and a college student.
The menu is surprisingly **diverse** for a small diner, with Korean, Mexican and Greek dishes.

drill.sentence: The coastline is home to a {{diverse}} range of birds, from tiny hummingbirds to huge pelicans.
drill.hint: full of many different kinds (not *wide*, *broad* or *varied*)

mistake.wrong: I have diverse questions about the contract.
mistake.right: I have several questions about the contract.
mistake.why: German *diverse* means *several* or *various*; English *diverse* means *very varied* and stresses difference.

entries.related: *varied* — of different kinds, neutral; *various* — several different; *mixed* — combining types, more casual; *homogeneous* — the opposite, all the same.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Not supporting or helping either side in a war, conflict, argument or competition.
entries.usage: Used for countries, referees, mediators, language and opinions: *remain neutral*, *stay neutral*, *a neutral observer*, *a neutral site*, *neutral language*. It sounds positive when fairness is expected, as from a judge, but can sound cowardly when someone avoids taking a side on purpose. It also describes colors (*neutral tones*) and the car gear.
entries.pattern: stay / remain neutral (in / on something); a neutral observer / site / tone
examples: Switzerland stayed **neutral** during both world wars.
The final will be played at a **neutral** site, so neither team has home-field advantage.
As a mediator, my job is to stay **neutral** and help both sides talk to each other.

drill.sentence: Two of my closest friends had a big falling-out, and I'm trying to remain {{neutral}} instead of picking a side.
drill.hint: on neither side (not *impartial* or *objective*)

entries.related: *impartial* — treating all sides equally, often of judges; *objective* — based on facts, not feelings; *nonpartisan* — not linked to a political party; *biased* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Causing a lot of public disagreement or strong opinions, because many people disapprove of it.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *a controversial decision*, *a controversial figure*, *a controversial topic*, *highly controversial*. It describes the thing or person that causes the argument, not the argument itself. To say people disagreed strongly, natives say *a heated debate* or *was hotly debated*.
entries.pattern: a controversial decision / topic / figure / call; highly controversial
examples: The referee's **controversial** call in the final seconds cost them the game.
Pineapple on pizza is a surprisingly **controversial** topic in our family.
The city's **controversial** plan to cut down two hundred old trees has been put on hold.

drill.sentence: The museum's decision to sell three famous paintings was highly {{controversial}}, and several board members resigned.
drill.hint: causing heated public argument (not *divisive*, *contentious* or *unpopular*)

mistake.wrong: The new plan was discussed very controversially at the meeting.
mistake.right: The new plan was hotly debated at the meeting.
mistake.why: German *kontrovers diskutieren* does not translate directly; a topic or decision is *controversial*, and the discussion is *heated*.

entries.related: *contentious* — likely to cause argument, more formal; *divisive* — splitting people into hostile groups; *polarizing* — producing two strong opposite views; *uncontroversial* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A heavy duty, responsibility, worry or cost that is hard to carry, especially one placed on a person or group.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *a burden on* someone, *a financial burden*, *the tax burden*, *ease the burden*, *the burden of proof*. People who need care often say *I don't want to be a burden*. It is serious in tone; for small annoyances, *hassle* or *pain* is more natural.
entries.pattern: a burden on / for someone; a financial burden; ease / share / shift the burden; the burden of proof
examples: After her surgery, my grandmother kept saying she didn't want to be a **burden** on us.
Student loans are a huge financial **burden** for many young families.
City officials say the new stadium won't add to the tax **burden** on local homeowners.

drill.sentence: The new daycare center should ease the {{burden}} on working parents in our neighborhood.
drill.hint: heavy weight of duties and costs (not *pressure*, *strain* or *load*)

entries.related: *load* — informal, an amount of work; *strain* — pressure that wears you down; *obligation* — a duty, without the heavy feeling; *relief* — what you feel when a burden is removed.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: After that; at a later time than the event just mentioned.
entries.usage: Formal and mostly written: news reports, police statements, résumés, histories and academic texts. It shows order in time, not cause; for a result, use *consequently*. In conversation natives say *later*, *after that* or *then*.
entries.pattern: subsequently + past verb; was subsequently + past participle
examples: The driver was arrested at the scene and **subsequently** charged with reckless driving.
Built in 1910 for one family, the house was **subsequently** divided into four apartments.
We met at a wedding in 2019 and **subsequently** discovered that we'd grown up two streets apart.

drill.sentence: The patient was taken to the ER with chest pain and was {{subsequently}} diagnosed with a minor heart attack.
drill.hint: after that, in formal style (not *later*, *then*, *afterward* or *eventually*)

entries.related: *consequently* — as a result; *later* / *afterward* — neutral, everyday; *previously* — the opposite, before that.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To produce or create something, such as income, electricity, ideas, interest or jobs.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and technical language: *generate revenue*, *generate income*, *generate jobs*, *generate interest*, *generate electricity*. It sounds more formal and impersonal than *make* or *bring in*. You *produce* or *make* goods, but you *generate* income, interest, ideas, heat or waste.
entries.pattern: generate revenue / income / jobs / interest / electricity / ideas
examples: Solar panels on the school roof **generate** enough electricity to power the gym.
The festival **generates** about two million dollars for local businesses every summer.
Her post about the lost dog **generated** hundreds of shares, and he was home by evening.

drill.sentence: The city hopes the new stadium will {{generate}} thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue.
drill.hint: cause to exist; a common business verb (not *create*, *bring* or *produce*)

entries.related: *produce* — make goods or results; *create* — bring into existence, broader; *bring in* — informal, for money; *spark* — for interest or debate.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Fair, reasonable and acceptable (*a legitimate concern*); also allowed by law or by the rules (*a legitimate business*).
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *a legitimate question*, *a legitimate concern*, *a legitimate reason*, *a legitimate business*. *That's a legitimate point* admits that the other person is right to raise something. The adjective ends in a weak *-mut*, and the short slang form *legit* (*Is this website legit?*) is very common in casual American speech.
entries.pattern: a legitimate concern / question / reason / complaint / business
examples: Asking how the money will be spent is a perfectly **legitimate** question.
Before you pay, check that the ticket seller is a **legitimate** business and not a scam.
The neighbors have a **legitimate** complaint; our dog barks all day while we're at work.

drill.sentence: Being stuck in a snowstorm is a {{legitimate}} excuse for missing a dentist appointment.
drill.hint: acceptable and fair (not *valid*, *good* or *reasonable*)

entries.related: *valid* — logically or legally sound; *justified* — having good reasons; *legit* — slang, real or acceptable; *illegitimate* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The quality of being honest and following strong moral principles, even when doing so costs you something.
entries.usage: Used in speech and writing, often as high praise: *a person of integrity*, *have integrity*, *personal integrity*, *academic integrity*, *question someone's integrity*. It suggests that what you say and what you do match. A second meaning is *being whole and undamaged*, as in *the structural integrity of a bridge*.
entries.pattern: a person of integrity; have / show integrity; question someone's integrity; academic integrity
examples: She's a woman of great **integrity**; she'd never lie to cover her own mistakes.
The coach showed real **integrity** when he reported his own team for breaking the recruiting rules.
Copying an essay from the internet is a serious violation of academic **integrity**.

drill.sentence: A good mechanic with {{integrity}} will tell you when a repair isn't worth the money.
drill.hint: a firm sense of right and wrong (not *honesty*, *principles* or *ethics*)

entries.related: *honesty* — telling the truth; *principles* — your moral rules; *character* — moral strength, broader; *corruption* — the opposite in public life.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An explanation or understanding of what something means, especially when other explanations are also possible.
entries.usage: Common in law, art, sports and everyday arguments: *my interpretation of*, *a different interpretation*, *open to interpretation*, *a strict* or *loose interpretation*. It suggests that the meaning depends partly on the person reading or watching. It also means spoken translation (*simultaneous interpretation*) and a performer's own version of a song or role.
entries.pattern: an interpretation of + noun; open to interpretation; a strict / loose / different interpretation
examples: The ending of the movie is open to **interpretation**; my wife and I argued about it all the way home.
The referee's **interpretation** of the new handball rule surprised everyone in the stadium.
Her **interpretation** of the old Beatles song is slower and much sadder than the original.

drill.sentence: The lease says "no pets," but under my landlord's loose {{interpretation}}, a goldfish is fine.
drill.hint: explanation of what the words mean (not *reading* or *definition*)

entries.related: *reading* — an interpretation, less formal (*my reading of the situation*); *translation* — of written text; *misinterpretation* — a wrong understanding.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A nervous, worried feeling that makes it hard to relax; also unfriendly feelings or conflict between people or groups that may lead to a fight.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *the tension in the room*, *ease the tension*, *tension between* two people or groups, *rising tensions*. In news, the plural *tensions* is typical for conflict between countries or communities. It is also used for tight muscles (*tension in my shoulders*).
entries.pattern: tension between A and B; ease / defuse / build tension; rising tensions
examples: You could feel the **tension** at dinner when my uncle brought up the inheritance.
There's been some **tension** between the new manager and the older staff.
**Tensions** between the two countries rose after a fishing boat was seized.

drill.sentence: The two neighbors haven't spoken since the fight over the fence, and the {{tension}} on our street is obvious.
drill.hint: unfriendly feeling between people (not *friction* or *hostility*)

entries.related: *stress* — pressure on one person; *friction* — conflict from disagreement; *strain* — pressure on a relationship; *suspense* — exciting uncertainty in a story.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To draw attention to something, or show clearly that it is important.
entries.usage: Very common in reports, news, presentations and meetings: *highlight a problem*, *highlight the need for*, *highlight the importance of*. An event or report can *highlight* a problem by making people notice it, so the subject is often not a person. Literally, it means marking text with a bright pen or color.
entries.pattern: highlight a problem / the need for / the importance of + noun
examples: The flooding last spring **highlighted** how old the town's drainage system is.
In your cover letter, **highlight** the experience that matches the job description.
The coach's speech **highlighted** the importance of rest days, not just hard training.

drill.sentence: The missing hiker's story {{highlights}} the need to tell someone where you're going before you head out.
drill.hint: makes it stand out; also what a yellow marker does (not *shows*, *stresses* or *underscores*)

entries.related: *emphasize* — give special importance in speech; *underline* / *underscore* — stress, more formal; *point out* — mention a fact; *downplay* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Easily hurt, harmed, attacked or influenced, physically or emotionally.
entries.usage: Common in news, health and personal talk: *vulnerable to* + noun (*vulnerable to infection*, *to attack*), *vulnerable groups*, *the most vulnerable*. *Feel vulnerable* or *make yourself vulnerable* is about showing your feelings, often in a positive sense in American self-help talk. In security, it means having weak points, and the noun *vulnerability* also means a security hole.
entries.pattern: vulnerable to + noun; vulnerable groups / people; feel vulnerable
examples: Older people are more **vulnerable** to heat stroke, so check on your neighbors during heat waves.
Telling him how I really felt made me feel incredibly **vulnerable**.
Old routers that never get updates are **vulnerable** to hackers.

drill.sentence: Newborn sea turtles are extremely {{vulnerable}} as they crawl across the beach to the ocean.
drill.hint: easy for predators to harm (not *exposed*, *fragile* or *defenseless*)

entries.related: *fragile* — easily broken; *exposed* — not protected; *susceptible to* — likely to be affected, for illness or influence; *resilient* — the opposite, recovers quickly.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To put a plan, decision, policy or system into action so that it starts working.
entries.usage: Typical in business, government, IT and project talk: *implement a plan*, *implement changes*, *implement a policy*, *implement a new system*. It refers to the practical work that follows a decision. The verb has a full last vowel (IM-pluh-ment); the noun *implement* (a tool) ends in a weak *-munt*.
entries.pattern: implement a plan / policy / changes / a system / recommendations
examples: The school will **implement** a new phone policy next fall: phones stay in lockers all day.
The restaurant **implemented** a reservation system after customers complained about long lines.
The city **implemented** the new parking rules without warning, and hundreds of drivers got tickets.

drill.sentence: The homeowners' association approved the new recycling rules in May but still hasn't {{implemented}} them.
drill.hint: actually put into action (not *enforced*, *applied* or *carried out*)

entries.related: *carry out* — do a task or plan, neutral; *execute* — carry out, often in business; *roll out* — introduce gradually to users; *enforce* — make people obey a rule.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To show clearly that something is true, using evidence or examples; also to show how something works or is done.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech and writing: *demonstrate that* + clause, *demonstrate how to*, *demonstrate a skill*, *demonstrate commitment*. In job applications and reviews it means *prove with actions* (*demonstrated leadership*). It also means to take part in a public protest (*demonstrate against*), so context decides.
entries.pattern: demonstrate that …; demonstrate how to + verb; demonstrate a skill / commitment / knowledge
examples: At the store, a salesman **demonstrated** the vacuum cleaner by pouring sand on the carpet and cleaning it up in seconds.
These figures clearly **demonstrate** that the new bus lanes have cut travel times.
He **demonstrated** his commitment to the team by playing through a broken finger.

drill.sentence: In the cooking class, the chef first {{demonstrated}} how to fold the dumplings, and then we tried it ourselves.
drill.hint: did it in front of us as an example (not *showed* or *explained*)

entries.related: *show* — the everyday word; *prove* — show beyond doubt; *illustrate* — make clear with examples; *protest* — the other sense of *demonstrate*.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very noticeable or unusual, so that you pay attention to it; about looks, attractive in an unusual way.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *a striking resemblance*, *a striking contrast*, *a striking example*, *what's striking is …*. About appearance, *a striking woman* or *striking eyes* means attractive in a memorable way. It also means *on strike* (*striking workers*), so context decides.
entries.pattern: a striking resemblance / contrast / example / difference; what's striking is …
examples: There's a **striking** resemblance between the two sisters, though they're five years apart.
What's most **striking** about the new library is how much natural light comes in.
She has **striking** green eyes that everyone notices right away.

drill.sentence: He isn't handsome in the usual way, but with his white hair and dark eyebrows, he's very {{striking}}.
drill.hint: unusual-looking in a way that catches your eye (not *stunning*, *distinctive* or *attractive*)

entries.related: *remarkable* — worth mentioning, often positive; *stark* — harsh and obvious; *noticeable* — weaker, easy to see; *stunning* — very beautiful.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Able to continue for a long time without damaging the environment or using up natural resources.
entries.usage: Very common in business, news, food and fashion: *sustainable energy*, *sustainable farming*, *sustainable fishing*, *sustainable materials*. It has become a marketing word, so it can sound vague or like *greenwashing*. It also simply means *able to continue* (*That workload isn't sustainable*).
entries.pattern: sustainable energy / farming / development / fishing / materials
examples: The restaurant buys only **sustainable** seafood from local fishermen.
We'd like to build a more **sustainable** house, with solar panels and good insulation.
The town wants to make tourism more **sustainable** by limiting cruise ship visits.

drill.sentence: This brand makes its jackets from recycled bottles and other {{sustainable}} materials.
drill.hint: kind to the environment over the long term (not *green*, *renewable* or *eco-friendly*)

entries.related: *renewable* — that can be replaced naturally (*renewable energy*); *eco-friendly* / *green* — informal; *sustainability* — the noun.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Happening or existing in many places, or among many people.
entries.usage: Common in news and formal writing: *widespread damage*, *widespread support*, *widespread belief*, *widespread use*, *widespread power outages*. It is often used for problems (*widespread fraud*), but also for good things (*widespread support*). It can go before a noun or after *be* (*The problem is widespread*).
entries.pattern: widespread damage / support / use / belief / outages
examples: Power outages were **widespread** after the storm, and some towns were dark for a week.
There's a **widespread** belief that you lose most of your body heat through your head, but it's a myth.
The plan to turn the old rail line into a bike path has **widespread** support in town.

drill.sentence: Smartphone use among ten-year-olds is now so {{widespread}} that schools are rewriting their rules.
drill.hint: found almost everywhere (not *common*, *prevalent* or *pervasive*)

entries.related: *common* — happening often, more general; *prevalent* — formal, common in a group; *pervasive* — spreading through everything; *rare* or *isolated* — the opposites.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A clear, deep understanding of a complex situation or person, or a new piece of understanding of that kind.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *insight into* + noun, *gain insight*, *offer* or *provide insight*, *a valuable insight*. It can be uncountable (*She has great insight*) or countable (*a few insights*). The preposition is *into*, not *in*; in business, *insights* also means useful conclusions from data.
entries.pattern: insight into + noun; gain / give / offer insight; a valuable / useful insight
examples: Living with a host family gave me real **insight** into everyday life in Japan.
My grandmother had a lot of **insight** into people; she could always tell who was lying.
Thanks for your **insights** at the meeting; they really changed how I see the problem.

drill.sentence: The documentary provides fascinating {{insight}} into the lives of long-haul truck drivers.
drill.hint: deep understanding (not *glimpse*)

mistake.wrong: The trip gave me real insight in American culture.
mistake.right: The trip gave me real insight into American culture.
mistake.why: *Insight* takes *into*; *in* is a common error, partly from German *Einblick in*.

entries.related: *understanding* — more general; *perspective* — a way of seeing; *glimpse* — a quick look or partial idea; *insightful* — the adjective, showing deep understanding.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A possible situation or series of events that might happen, especially one you imagine in order to plan for it.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in everyday talk: *the worst-case scenario*, *the best-case scenario*, *in that scenario*, *a likely* or *realistic scenario*. In planning, people *run through* or *consider* different scenarios. In speech, *Worst-case scenario, …* at the start of a sentence means *If the worst happens, …*.
entries.pattern: a worst-case / best-case scenario; in this / that scenario; a likely / realistic scenario
examples: Worst-case **scenario**, it rains all weekend and we play board games in the cabin.
Let's think through a **scenario** where both of us lose our jobs at the same time.
Experts say a major earthquake in the region is a realistic **scenario** within the next thirty years.

drill.sentence: The best-case {{scenario}} is that the repair takes two days; the worst case is a new engine.
drill.hint: imagined situation (not *outcome*)

entries.related: *situation* — what actually exists now; *outcome* — the final result; *contingency* — a possible future event you prepare for, formal.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To admit or accept that something is true, real or exists, often when you would prefer not to.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech, writing and serious conversation: *acknowledge that* + clause, *acknowledge a mistake*, *acknowledge the problem*, *widely acknowledged*. It is more formal than *admit* and often sounds fair or diplomatic. It also means to show you have noticed someone (*She didn't even acknowledge me*) or received something (*acknowledge receipt*).
entries.pattern: acknowledge that …; acknowledge a mistake / a problem / someone's help; be widely acknowledged as
examples: To his credit, the coach **acknowledged** that he'd made the wrong substitution.
The first step is to **acknowledge** that you have a problem with money.
She is widely **acknowledged** as one of the best pastry chefs in the country.

drill.sentence: The airline finally {{acknowledged}} that the delays were its own fault, not the weather's.
drill.hint: openly agreed it was true (not *admitted*, *accepted*, *confirmed* or *conceded*)

entries.related: *admit* — more common, often about guilt; *concede* — admit in an argument, reluctantly; *recognize* — accept officially; *deny* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Easy to reach, enter, use or understand, including for people with disabilities.
entries.usage: Common in everyday and official language: *wheelchair accessible*, *accessible by public transit*, *accessible to* + people, *an accessible book*. In American usage it very often means built for people with disabilities: ramps, elevators, wide doors. About books, talks and art, it means easy to understand without special knowledge, which is usually praise.
entries.pattern: accessible to + people; accessible by car / boat / transit; wheelchair accessible
examples: Is the theater **accessible**? My dad uses a wheelchair.
The beach is only **accessible** by boat, which keeps it quiet even in July.
The book explains black holes in a way that's **accessible** to middle school kids.

drill.sentence: The hotel says all of its first-floor rooms are fully wheelchair {{accessible}}.
drill.hint: easy to get into and use (not *friendly*)

entries.related: *available* — ready to use or buy; *reachable* — can be reached, more literal; *user-friendly* — easy to use, for products; *inaccessible* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An unfair preference for or against a person, group or idea that affects your judgment.
entries.usage: Common in news, law, research and everyday arguments: *bias against*, *bias toward* or *in favor of*, *unconscious bias*, *confirmation bias*. It is a criticism, so accusing someone of *bias* is serious. The adjective is *biased* (*a biased referee*), with *-ed*.
entries.pattern: bias against / toward / in favor of + noun; unconscious / confirmation bias
examples: Some parents complained about the judge's **bias** toward dancers from her own studio.
I have a slight **bias** toward Italian food, so don't let me choose the restaurant again.
The study tried to reduce **bias** by not telling the doctors which patients got the real drug.

drill.sentence: Hiring managers often have an unconscious {{bias}} against older applicants with long gaps in their résumés.
drill.hint: unfair leaning (not *prejudice*)

mistake.why: *Bias* is the noun; the adjective needs *-ed*: *biased*.

entries.related: *prejudice* — unfair dislike, usually of a group, stronger; *partiality* — formal, favoring one side; *objectivity* — the opposite; *biased* — the adjective.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The way a person or the public sees, understands or judges something, which may be different from the facts.
entries.usage: Common in business, politics and psychology: *public perception*, *the perception that* + clause, *change the perception of*. *Perception is reality* is a common saying at work, meaning that what people believe matters more than the facts. It also means the ability to notice things through the senses (*depth perception*).
entries.pattern: the perception that …; public perception of + noun; change / shape perceptions
examples: There's a common **perception** that city people are unfriendly, but my neighbors are wonderful.
The new ads are trying to change the public **perception** of the brand as old-fashioned.
Your **perception** of time changes when you have kids; the years go by so fast.

drill.sentence: The {{perception}} that the neighborhood is dangerous keeps buyers away, even though crime has dropped.
drill.hint: the way people see it, true or not (not *belief*, *idea*, *fear* or *impression*)

entries.related: *impression* — an opinion formed quickly; *view* — an opinion; *image* — how a person or brand is seen; *reality* — often contrasted with *perception*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To find a solution to a problem, or to settle a disagreement or argument so that it ends.
entries.usage: Common in work, customer service, law and news: *resolve an issue*, *resolve a dispute*, *resolve a conflict*, *resolve a complaint*. It sounds more formal and final than *fix* or *sort out*. The noun is *resolution*; a *New Year's resolution* uses a different sense, a firm decision.
entries.pattern: resolve an issue / a problem / a dispute / a conflict / a complaint; be resolved
examples: Our internet has been down for three days, and the company still hasn't **resolved** the issue.
Most family arguments can be **resolved** with a calm conversation and a bit of humor.
The players' union and the league **resolved** their differences just before the season started.

drill.sentence: It took a lawyer and two long meetings to {{resolve}} the dispute over the strip of land between our houses.
drill.hint: formal verb: find an agreed solution to (not *settle*, *end* or *sort out*)

entries.related: *solve* — find the answer to a problem or puzzle; *settle* — end an argument or legal case; *sort out* — informal; *resolution* — the noun.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Real and important but not obvious, because it lies beneath the surface; forming the basis of something.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, analysis and serious discussion: *the underlying cause*, *an underlying problem*, *underlying issues*, *an underlying condition*. It contrasts the visible symptom with the deeper reason, as in *treat the underlying cause, not just the symptoms*. As an adjective it comes before the noun; the verb is *underlie* (*the problems that underlie the crisis*).
entries.pattern: the underlying cause / problem / issue / condition / reason
examples: Older patients with **underlying** heart conditions are at higher risk during heat waves.
The fight about the dishes was really about an **underlying** problem: they both felt overworked.
Painting over the stain won't help if you don't fix the **underlying** leak.

drill.sentence: The headaches turned out to be just a symptom; the {{underlying}} cause was a problem with her eyesight.
drill.hint: hidden beneath the surface (not *real*, *true*, *root* or *actual*)

entries.related: *root* — basic, in *root cause*; *fundamental* — basic and important; *hidden* — not seen; *superficial* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An idea or belief about something, often one that is vague, wrong or not fully thought through.
entries.usage: Common in discussion and writing: *the notion that* + clause, *reject the notion*, *a romantic notion*, *preconceived notions*. It often signals doubt or criticism, as in *the notion that money buys happiness*. It is more formal than *idea*; *preconceived notions* are fixed ideas you have before you know the facts.
entries.pattern: the notion that …; reject / challenge the notion; a vague / romantic notion; preconceived notions
examples: She had a romantic **notion** of farm life until she spent a summer milking cows at 5 a.m.
I reject the **notion** that kids today are lazier than we were.
Try to visit without any preconceived **notions**; the city surprises most people.

drill.sentence: He laughed at the {{notion}} that a dog could be trained to call 911.
drill.hint: an idea he found silly (not *idea*, *thought*, *claim* or *suggestion*)

entries.related: *idea* — the everyday word; *concept* — an abstract idea, often precise; *belief* — something you hold true; *misconception* — a wrong idea.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To keep or continue to have something, such as staff, customers, heat, water or information.
entries.usage: Common in business, HR, science and formal writing: *retain staff*, *retain customers*, *retain heat*, *retain moisture*, *retain information*, *retain control*. It sounds more formal than *keep* and stresses that something could be lost. Americans also *retain a lawyer*, meaning hire one; the noun is *retention* (*customer retention*).
entries.pattern: retain staff / customers / talent / control; retain heat / water / information
examples: Cast-iron pans **retain** heat for a long time, so be careful when you serve from them.
The hospital is struggling to **retain** nurses, many of whom leave after two years.
I read the chapter twice, but I didn't **retain** a single thing.

drill.sentence: Add a little mulch around the tomatoes to help the soil {{retain}} moisture during dry weeks.
drill.hint: avoid losing (formal; not *keep* or *hold*)

entries.related: *keep* — the everyday word; *maintain* — keep at the same level; *preserve* — protect from change or damage; *retention* — the noun.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To accept a new idea, change, opportunity or way of life willingly and with enthusiasm.
entries.usage: Common in business, journalism and personal talk: *embrace change*, *embrace technology*, *embrace a challenge*, *embrace a new culture*. It is warmer and more enthusiastic than *accept*, and it is frequent in corporate language, where it can sound like a slogan. Its literal sense, *hug*, is more formal or written.
entries.pattern: embrace change / a new idea / technology / the opportunity
examples: My grandmother has fully **embraced** video calls; she calls us every Sunday now.
Moving to Texas was hard at first, but we've really **embraced** the slower pace of life.
Companies that **embrace** remote work often find it easier to hire.

drill.sentence: Instead of fighting her gray hair, she decided to {{embrace}} it and stopped dyeing it.
drill.hint: welcome it gladly (not *accept* or *own*)

entries.related: *accept* — agree to, without enthusiasm; *welcome* — receive gladly; *adopt* — start using; *reject* or *resist* — the opposites.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Coming before the main or final part of something; early and not yet final or complete.
entries.usage: Common in news, science, law and sports: *preliminary results*, *preliminary findings*, *a preliminary report*, *a preliminary hearing*, *preliminary talks*. It warns that more information or a final decision will follow. The plural noun *preliminaries* means early steps or small talk (*skip the preliminaries*).
entries.pattern: preliminary results / findings / report / talks / hearing / round
examples: According to **preliminary** reports, nobody was seriously hurt in the crash.
**Preliminary** results suggest the new drug lowers blood pressure, but larger trials are needed.
She won her **preliminary** heat easily and will swim in the final on Saturday.

drill.sentence: The suspect will appear in court next week for a {{preliminary}} hearing.
drill.hint: early, before the main trial (not *first*, *initial* or *pretrial*)

entries.related: *initial* — first, at the beginning; *provisional* — temporary until confirmed; *final* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make a determined effort to deal with a difficult problem or task.
entries.usage: Common in news, work and everyday talk: *tackle a problem*, *tackle an issue*, *tackle a project*, *tackle the dishes*. It sounds active and determined, as if you are attacking the problem. In football and soccer it has its literal meaning, *tackle a player*.
entries.pattern: tackle a problem / an issue / a project / a task
examples: The city has promised to **tackle** the potholes on Elm Street before winter.
I'm finally going to **tackle** the garage this weekend; you can't even park in there.
The new coach wants to **tackle** the team's problem with turnovers first.

drill.sentence: Rather than trying to fix everything at once, let's {{tackle}} the biggest issue first: the leaking roof.
drill.hint: start working hard on (not *fix*, *address*, *handle* or *deal with*)

entries.related: *address* — formal, start dealing with; *deal with* / *handle* — neutral; *take on* — accept a challenge; *avoid* or *put off* — the opposites.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To remove or get rid of something completely; also to rule something out as a possibility.
entries.usage: Common in health, business and investigations: *eliminate waste*, *eliminate the risk*, *eliminate the need for*, *eliminate sugar from your diet*, *eliminate a suspect*. *Eliminate* + noun + *from* + noun is a frequent pattern. In sports, *be eliminated* means knocked out of a competition.
entries.pattern: eliminate + noun (from + noun); eliminate the need / risk; eliminate a possibility / suspect
examples: My doctor told me to **eliminate** sugary drinks from my diet completely.
Police were able to **eliminate** him as a suspect because he was at work all night.
Automatic payments **eliminate** the risk of forgetting a bill.

drill.sentence: Washing your hands well won't {{eliminate}} the risk of catching a cold, but it lowers it a lot.
drill.hint: reduce to zero (not *remove* or *get rid of*)

entries.related: *remove* — take away, neutral; *get rid of* — informal; *rule out* — decide something is not possible; *reduce* — make smaller, not to zero.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To give good reasons that show a decision, action or cost is right or reasonable.
entries.usage: Common at work and in everyday arguments: *justify a decision*, *justify the cost*, *justify* + *-ing*, *justify yourself*. It often appears in negative or doubting sentences: *I can't justify spending that much*, *How do you justify …?* The adjective *justified* means *with good reason* (*Her anger was justified*).
entries.pattern: justify a decision / the cost / an expense; justify + -ing; justify yourself
examples: I love that coat, but I can't **justify** spending $400 on it right now.
How does the airline **justify** charging fifty dollars for a carry-on bag?
You don't have to **justify** yourself to me; I was just curious.

drill.sentence: The school board had to {{justify}} the huge cost of the new football field to angry parents.
drill.hint: make a case that it was right (not *explain* or *defend*)

entries.related: *explain* — give reasons, without saying they are good; *defend* — argue for something under attack; *excuse* — make a fault seem less bad; *justification* — the noun.
